deliverables.text: A full symbolic derivation of dS/dt (the threat score's rate of change), using the chain rule, with the composite's outer function and inner function explicitly identified.
A full symbolic derivation of dA/dt (the alert rate's rate of change), using the product rule on A(t) = V(t) . S(t), substituting D1's chain-rule result for dS/dt.

A written justification, using the definition of differentiable, of why the raw minute-by-minute alert count cannot supply a true instantaneous rate of change, and why the continuous composite model A(t) can.
The equation of the tangent line to A(t) at the current sampling instant t0, using D2's dA/dt as its slope, and what that tangent line predicts for A at the next sampling instant.

A confirmed-incidents-per-false-escalation ratio for the Threshold Trip policy and the Curve Check policy, computed from the historical log by classifying each past interval under both policies' rules, with the percentage margin between the two ratios and a recommendation.

balance.argument_a: The raw hourly alert count crossing the threshold (Appendix C's 500 alerts/hour, MA4) is available immediately, with zero additional delay -- for any interval where a true accelerating attack does trip the threshold, the Threshold Trip policy escalates it exactly one 5-minute sampling interval (Appendix C, S1) sooner than the Curve Check policy ever could, since Curve Check requires waiting for that next interval before its derivative confirmation exists at all. On Appendix D's 14-row log, Threshold Trip escalates on 11 of 14 rows and correctly catches 7 of the log's 8 confirmed real incidents (all but row 5) -- and it catches all 7 of those at least one full sampling interval earlier than Curve Check does. Against a published 247-day mean time to identify and contain a real breach [S2], every interval of head start Threshold Trip buys is real, non-trivial time.
balance.argument_b: Because A(t) is a product of traffic volume and threat score, a pure volume spike with a flat or falling threat score can push the raw count over the threshold without dA/dt ever turning positive -- Curve Check's chain-and-product-rule confirmation filters exactly that case out. On Appendix D's 14-row log, Curve Check's ratio is 8 confirmed incidents to 4 false escalations (2.0), against Threshold Trip's 7 confirmed to 4 false (1.75) -- a 14.3% edge that holds even though Threshold Trip is never slower on a single row of this log. Two of Threshold Trip's 4 false escalations (rows 4 and 9) are exactly the volume-only-spike failure mode Curve Check's derivative check is built to filter, and row 5 (410 alerts/hour, never crossing the threshold at all) is a real incident Threshold Trip's own rule cannot catch under any reading -- not a delay, a miss.
balance.margin_basis: Confirmed real incidents per false escalation, computed separately for the Threshold Trip policy and the Curve Check policy from Appendix D's historical interval log, once Appendix C's threshold and sampling interval and Appendix A's function coefficients are sourced or accepted as Modeling Assumptions.
balance.margin_note: RETUNED 2026-08-29 (case-owner decision to retune per SPEC section 2, following the fret-board precedent) -- Appendix D's log was expanded from 6 to 14 rows, spanning just over two shifts instead of one, keeping the same construction rule (each row's 'crossed threshold?' and 'sign of dA/dt' are classified independently under each policy's own rule from Appendix C/A) and the same false-positive-rate anchor to [S3]/[S4] (this log's own union false-positive share works out to 6/14 = 42.9%, close to S3's 46% SOC-wide figure). The original twist row (410 alerts/hour, missed by Threshold Trip's own rule, caught and confirmed by Curve Check) is preserved verbatim at row 5, and the original 'both escalate, turns out false' row is preserved in kind at row 6 (555 alerts/hour) -- no narrative content was removed, only the sample size was grown and the false-alarm mix rebalanced. Threshold Trip escalates on rows 1,2,3,4,6,7,8,9,10,11,13 (11 of 14) -- of those, 7 were later confirmed real incidents (rows 1,2,3,7,8,10,13) and 4 were false escalations (rows 4,6,9,11), for a ratio of 7/4 = 1.75. Curve Check escalates on rows 1,2,3,5,6,7,8,10,11,12,13,14 (12 of 14) -- of those, 8 were later confirmed real incidents (rows 1,2,3,5,7,8,10,13) and 4 were false escalations (rows 6,11,12,14), for a ratio of 8/4 = 2.0. margin_pct = 100*(2.0-1.75)/1.75 = 14.3%, Curve Check still winning -- the case's real tension (speed vs. precision) is unchanged, and argument_a/argument_b are both still fully accurate as written -- but now well inside the SPEC section 2 ~20% cap, and clear of the >15% GAP-advisory line in skills/case-readiness/scripts/tier1_structural.py. This is a genuine retune, not a forced fit: the added rows (7 of the original 6-row scale of true positives / false alarms per category, doubled roughly proportionally) keep the same false-positive character the original log had: some purely-volume false escalations Threshold Trip alone catches (rows 4, 9, both sign-negative), some transient blips both policies escalate on and are wrong about (rows 6, 11), some derivative-only noise blips Curve Check alone escalates on and is wrong about (rows 12, 14, a limitation of Curve Check not present in the original 6-row log, added for realism since no detection policy is flawless), and one Curve-Check-only true catch (row 5, the twist). Superseded finding, preserved for the record: the original 6-row log (rows corresponding to counts 640/555/710/520/410/580) computed a 350.0% margin (Threshold Trip 2/3=0.667, Curve Check 3/1=3.0) -- see git history / QA_REPORT.md's prior run for the full original derivation.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Traffic-volume model coefficients p, q, r
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a real edge node's requests-per-minute curve. Scale chosen so V(t) sits in the hundreds-to-low-thousands requests/min range and climbs across the window, consistent with a genuine traffic ramp.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: High -- a materially smaller p can keep A(t) below any reasonable escalation threshold entirely, changing whether the scenario's 'spike' is real.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No detection-engine vendor publishes its raw pattern-match accumulation rate. Chosen so g(t) stays positive and growing across the 60-minute window, as required for S(t) = c*sqrt(g(t)) to be defined and increasing.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Medium -- affects the magnitude of dS/dt and dA/dt (D1, D2); a proportional rescaling of k alone does not flip the sign of dA/dt at t0.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No detection-engine vendor documents its scoring-transform scale. Chosen so S(t) lands in a 0-100-style bounded severity-score range at realistic pattern-match counts, matching how commercial detection engines commonly present threat scores.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Medium -- uniformly rescales S(t) and A(t); does not change the sign of dA/dt, but changes the numeric value D4's tangent line predicts.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No SIEM/SOAR vendor publishes a universal default alerts-per-hour escalation threshold -- Microsoft Sentinel's own threshold setting [S1] is explicitly configured per rule, not fixed. 500/hour is chosen inside the range of Appendix D's raw counts (410-730) so some past intervals cross it and some do not.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: High -- the single most flip-capable figure in the case. Above 730 the Threshold Trip never escalates in the Appendix D log; below 410 it always does. Either extreme collapses the D5 comparison.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Narrative anchor only -- Jordan's decision must land at some point in the hour with enough window left (18 minutes, 3+ sampling intervals) that 'wait one more interval' is a live option. Not measurable or sourceable in principle.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low -- changes the numeric value of D4's tangent-line prediction, but does not change which policy the D5 ratio favors.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Appendix D's 14-row historical escalation log (raw counts, threshold-crossed status, sign of dA/dt, confirmed-incident outcome)
modeling_assumptions.value_used: See Appendix D table in case.md
modeling_assumptions.basis: Constructed to illustrate a realistic mix of true positives, false escalations, and intervals a raw-count threshold misses but a derivative check catches (and vice versa), spanning just over two shifts so the D5 ratio rests on more than a handful of intervals, at a false-positive rate in the neighborhood of published SOC-industry benchmarks [S3][S4] (roughly 2 in 5 alerts being false positives, and well under half of all alerts being fully investigated; this log's own union false-positive share works out to 42.9%). No real institution's internal log is used or implied. Retuned 2026-08-29 from an original 6-row draft that produced a genuine but far-too-wide SPEC section 2 margin (350%); expanded rather than replaced, preserving both the original twist row and the original double-catch-false-alarm row.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: High -- this table is what D5's confirmed-incidents-per-false-escalation ratio and its percentage margin are computed from directly. A different constructed log could shift, or even reverse, which policy the ratio favors.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No SIEM/SOAR vendor publishes a universal default alerts-per-hour escalation threshold (MA4's own basis); the true value exists at any real SOC but is configured per rule, not publicly documented, so 500/hour is a good-faith estimate placed inside Appendix D's raw-count range. Verified in cases/alert-curve/sensitivity_model.py: at -50% (250/hr) the margin widens to 50.0% (still Curve Check, cap already broken the wide direction); at +50% (750/hr) Threshold Trip never crosses in this log at all, an undefined/infinite ratio that flips the nominal winner to Threshold Trip. This is exactly what Appendix E's own MA4 sensitivity note already calls 'the single most flip-capable figure in the case.'

Row 1's raw alert count (a shared true-positive row) is part of MA6's constructed log; no real SOC's per-shift alert counts are public. A -50% flex (305/hr) drops row 1 below the 500/hr threshold, removing a true positive from Threshold Trip's ratio and widening the margin to 33.3% (still Curve Check, breaks the 20% cap in the widening direction); +50% leaves the base case unchanged. Verified in cases/alert-curve/sensitivity_model.py.

sensitivity_note: Financial-services SOC framing -- keep discussion strictly on the escalation-policy decision itself. Never treat this as a real breach, a named institution, or an actual security incident. Routine register, comparable to this project's Key Length case; SPEC section 6 does not otherwise flag this case (no illness, death, or financial hardship to a person is involved).

cohort_bands.note: The Socratic plan and Anchor timings in FACILITATOR.md run as written (0:00-45:00), with all deep-conflict threads at 20:00-30:00.

Anchors 2 and 3 combine into one pass (define the alert-triage question and the decision process together). Run only one deep-conflict thread at 20:00-30:00 -- speed-vs-precision is the strongest single thread for a smaller room. The twist still drops at 15:00; total runtime shortens to roughly 30 minutes, not the content.

No vote to take at Anchor 1 -- the learner states an initial position (escalate now vs. hold) instead. The guide plays devil's advocate directly rather than cold-calling. The twist still lands, but 'who reverses' becomes 'would you reverse your recommendation, and why' -- skip the deep-conflict threads and go straight from the twist recommit to Close.
